newsitem.title: USA: Cold storage data seen supportive to CME meats.
newsitem.headline: Cold storage data seen supportive to CME meats.

text.p: U.S. cold storage figures released by the U.S. Department of Agriculture were considered supportive to Chicago Mercantile Exchange meat futures. But daily fundamentals and a hog report next Friday will likely have more effect on markets, livestock analysts said.

They considered the decline of 30 million lbs in total pork supplies from the month, near historic low pork belly stocks and lower beef stocks as supporting factors for meat pits on Monday. But pork markets will likely pay more attention to the quarterly Hogs and Pigs report due for release next Friday then storage supplies.
"That (hog report) is going to dictate a lot more in the term of pricing strategies," said Chuck Levitt, senior livestock analyst for Alaron Trading Corp.

But the storage figures were somewhat of a surprise even though they were above last year's level. The decline from April to May was not anticipated in light of the Taiwan pork ban and expected increased pork exports to Japan. Total pork stocks declined to 410 million lbs during May from 440 million in April.
"I suspect after the disappointment they (packers) had in April (selling pork) there was not as much enthusiasm to load the boat, so to speak, in May as we really thought was happening" Levitt said.
However, large ham stocks will limit any support from low pork stocks in hog futures and the upcoming hog report will have more effect on that market, analysts said.

Pork belly futures were called 0.500 to 1.000 cent per lb higher on Monday following the report which showed pork belly stocks on May 31 at the second lowest number on record. Stocks of 55.713 million lbs fell in the early analyst range of 53.7 to 57.7 million but was only slightly above the old record May 31 low of 54.98 million.
Analysts said the slight increase of 1.3 million lbs during May compares with an increase of 6.3 million lbs during the same period last year.

"A lot of those bellies a year ago were stored in non-reporting warehouses whereas this year we didn't change much in those non-reporting warehouse numbers," said Dale Durchholz, AgriVisor Services Inc market analyst.

But Durchholz, as well as other analysts, was not that bullish over the low number of bellies in storage as the industry has been turing to increased use of fresh product and much of the storings could be attributed to reduced production instead of increased demand.
"We had a six percent decline in production during May then we had last year - and you also have less people relying on storage bellies," Levitt said.

The new boneless beef contracts may benefit from the report which showed frozen beef stocks down nearly five million lbs during the month to 280.7 million lbs versus 285.4 million in April and 307.4 million in storage last year.

The eight percent smaller supply of beef is a reflection of greater usage this year than last because of reduced cow slaughter this year. More of the imports of Australian and New Zealand beef were likely used to fill demand, analysts said.
But even here analyts saw little effect on the beef and cattle markets.
It is constructive to boneless beef "but I don't look at it as dramatically favorable," said Dale Benson, Vice President and senior livestock analyst for Dean Witter.
